Our last [letter] to Your Honors was dated the 23rd of October in the year 1635, whereby Your Honors were then informed of the abundant supply of all manner of Chinese goods, and that the trade in Taijuan began to show itself so much better over time, together with the good hope and appearance that there was to humble the pride of those from Mattanw [Mataram] and Soulangh [Surabaya], and to avenge the great injustice committed against ours in the time of the late Mr. Nuijts [Nuyts]. Item, what cargoes were sent in the previous southern monsoon to Japan and in the beginning of the northern monsoon to Batavia [Jakarta], namely: In the year 1635, on the 19th of August and 20th of the same month, by the ships Nieuw Amsterdam, Wassenaer, and Groe to Japan, one cargo was loaded together. On the 29th of the same month, by the yacht Venhuijse, as before, to Japan, one similar [cargo] was loaded. The following are the cargoes from Taijuan to Japan and from Batavia sent in various dates, namely: On the 6th of August, by the ships Wassenaer and the Galjas van Hoorn, which together with the Tercel and the small yacht Wateroose were sent on the 19th of July over Manila in the Pescadores [Piscadores], arrived and there cargoes were fully loaded, together with the yacht Grol to Japan ƒ 636837„13„1 their cargo amounting together. - On the 15th of the same month, by the fluyt ships Schagen, Swaen, and Huijsduijnen, as before, to Japan, their cargo amounting to „ 725836„1„7 On the 7th of October, by the ships Cerel and Bommel to Batavia, again the Pescadores sent, a return amounting together.

New supply of cash from Japan. Pleasant news from Japan. And there remained upon the departure of the fluyt ship Huijsduijne in Taijuan still too few ships, approximately 4000 picul [picul: a unit of weight, approximately 60 kg] of powder sugar, by shortage of ships to transport the same from Taijuan for the returns to Batavia, moreover, we had certain news from the Honorable Chincheo [Zhangzhou] that there, together with one richly laden silk junk, still eleven junks with sugar and other various kinds of merchant goods, not only had lain clear for a considerable time, but had already run out two to three times to advance their journey to Taijuan, but by storm each time were forced to return again into the aforementioned river, with which aforementioned junks good quantity of raw silk, many silk fabrics, and approximately 4 to 5 O:

--- CHUNK 1 ---
At the High [uncertain: H:e] Chincheo [Zhangzhou], there lay not only a richly laden silk junk, but also eleven junks with sugar and other various kinds of merchandise, which had not only lain there clear for a considerable time, but had already made two or three attempts to proceed on their journey to Taiwan [Tayouan], but each time were forced by storm to return into the aforementioned river. With these aforementioned junks there were good quantities of raw silk, many silk fabrics, and approximately four to five hundred piculs [modern equivalent: approximately 240-300 tons] of refined sugar, as well as other various merchandise that were waiting to be received in Taiwan, so that if the storm winds had not prevented it, and if there had been no shortage of ships there, a return shipment of Chinese merchandise serviceable for the Netherlands to Batavia [modern equivalent: Jakarta] could have returned in good time, by which Your Excellency could easily measure how the Chinese trade increases and improves daily. And the aforementioned free ships, the Galjas [uncertain: ship name], schagen [uncertain: ship type], and huijsduijnen [uncertain: ship type], came from Japan to Taiwan on the 10th of November, God be praised, at the desired time well arrived. A return cargo amounted to ƒ 1,039,888: 6: 11: [modern equivalent: Dutch guilders], consisting mostly of Japanese coinage and other necessities with which Taiwan was again excellently reinforced, in order to await the further relief, which we estimate (including five tons of gold that will be lifted as a deposit in Japan at the end of the monsoon, and drawn back ƒ 670,000:—:—: which from Japan will be sent to Batavia, Siam, Quinam [uncertain: location], and Oucquijt [uncertain: location]) will still amount to approximately twenty tons of gold, with which then the new purchases for Japan, the Fatherland, and all of India can be made. Which aforementioned ships from Japan (for which thanks must be given to the Almighty) learned the very pleasant and desired news of Your Excellency's affairs and commerce there. Namely, during the absence of President Conckebacker, the chief merchant Caron with the gifts in order to

--- CHUNK 2 ---
Japan approximately will be sent) will still amount to approximately twenty tons of gold, with which then the new purchases for Japan, the Fatherland, and all of India can be made. Which aforementioned ships from Japan (for which thanks must be given to the Almighty) learned the very pleasant and desired news of Your Excellency's affairs and commerce there. Namely, during the absence of President Conckebacker, the chief merchant Caron with the gifts in order to perform the yearly reverence for His Imperial Majesty went up to Jedo [modern equivalent: Tokyo], and after remaining there for some days appeared before His Majesty at court with pleasantness. The Emperor, who was pleased with the gifts (but particularly with the copper crown), had accepted them, but the imperial councillors did not dare to receive theirs in public, but they were sent to them in closed caskets at home. All further limitations in the Company's trade, as well as the request of the heads of the five imperial cities to obtain the Company's silk under lock and key (as was done with the Portuguese), was rejected with harsh reproaches by the Emperor's name through the council lord Sannickedome [uncertain: title/name]. Our cargoes from the first arriving ships had no more license to request from the regents of Nagasaki [Nangasacquij], but only (as had been the manner before) from those of Firando [modern equivalent: Hirado]. That our ships from Japan may depart as soon as they are loaded and ready, without waiting for the Portuguese, under the condition that the Macau galleons between Japan and Macau may not attack or capture us. That various excellent Japanese merchants had their request to trade in Sunchin [Soncquijn], Quinam, and Cambodia [Cambardja], as before, flatly rejected and denied. That His Imperial Majesty, having had the aforementioned copper crown hung by his father's grave in a place called Nikko [Nijcko], approximately four miles from Jedo,

--- CHUNK 3 ---
ready, without waiting for the Portuguese, under the condition that the Macau galleons between Japan and Macau may not attack or capture us. That various excellent Japanese merchants had their request to trade in Sunchin [Soncquijn], Quinam, and Cambodia [Cambardja], as before, flatly rejected and denied. That His Imperial Majesty, having had the aforementioned copper crown hung by his father's grave in a place called Nikko [Nijcko], approximately four miles from Jedo, when visiting the aforementioned grave saw the crown again, and considering to depart from Japan, asked why it was sent with such haste as was transported from Japan in the year 1636. The council lord Sannickedome charged the Hollanders to present in return 200 silver schouten [uncertain: unit of currency], amounting to ƒ 3,451:—:—: [modern equivalent: Dutch guilders], which gift is held in very high esteem by the Japanese nation, inasmuch as such a thing happens very rarely or seldom. That the Honorable Pieter Nuijts, at the request of the aforementioned council lord (who had undertaken this upon the occasion of presenting it to His Imperial Majesty), was released from his detention by Pieter Nuijts and licensed to depart, His Imperial Majesty giving the following reasons: the humble mission of the Governor in Japan has given me satisfaction, therefore I release him and forgive his mistreatment, and I allow that he may depart with the first ships to his land, which also took effect accordingly. Moreover, the governors of Nagasaki [Nangasacquij] with great pleasantness—the governors of Nagasaki—came to inspect our ships in Firando [Hirado], marveling at the strength and the power with which our ships can do things, further alleging why we marvel, we inspect with such nine ships the Spaniard of Formosa [Taiwan] not struck, that it would be pleasing to His Imperial Majesty, ours further answered that more merchants would bring goods there, in order to carry as much silver from there as the Spaniard to Japan as according to their

pleasantness the governors of Nagasaki came to inspect our ships in Firando [Hirado], marveling at the strength and the power with which our ships can do things, further alleging why we marvel, we inspect with such nine ships the Spaniard of Formosa [Taiwan] not struck, that it would be pleasing to His Imperial Majesty, ours further answered that more merchants would bring goods there, in order to carry as much silver from there as the Spaniard to Japan as according to their account the Portuguese did, who that year were not driven from Formosa, according to the letter of the Honorable Houckebacker. Beyond their derived debts, from Japan would not have been transported ƒ 66,976,500:—, which is more than twice as much as from our merchants with the profit of what capital with the Portuguese ƒ 1,421,966: 9: 8: (which in the year 1636 fell to ƒ 1,593,011: 1: 3: capital in Japan) proceeded, so that between us and the Portuguese over one hundred tons of gold in merchandise were sold that year there, whereby Your Excellency can measure what consideration (with the opening of the Chinese trade) the Japanese commerce also is. And so Your Excellency regarding the further matters that transpired there will be notified in detail and at length by the General letter, and also various Japanese papers will be sent to the Honorable Seventeen [the governing body of the VOC] in order to avoid tedium, we will conduct ourselves further as specified before. As was specified before, under the responsibility of the chief merchant Ducker, with the ships Warmont and Grol to Quinam (inasmuch as the Japanese were forbidden by the Emperor's Mandate to navigate to no quarters of India with their junks anymore) sent a capital amounting to ƒ 115,762: 2: 12: [modern equivalent: Dutch guilders], consisting mostly of copper senes [a certain currency much sought after there], little cash, other small necessities needed to make gifts to the King, so that the aforementioned senes or capital against good quantities of Quinam and Tonkin [Toncquijn] silk, as well as silk fabrics falling there,

the ships Warmont and Grol to Quinam (inasmuch as the Japanese were forbidden by the Emperor's Mandate to navigate to no quarters of India with their junks anymore) sent a capital amounting to ƒ 115,762: 2: 12: [modern equivalent: Dutch guilders], consisting mostly of copper senes [a certain currency much sought after there], little cash, other small necessities needed to make gifts to the King, so that the aforementioned senes or capital against good quantities of Quinam and Tonkin [Toncquijn] silk, as well as silk fabrics falling there, and also large quantities of brown sugar to be sold, as well as with the aforementioned 23,580 rixdollars [modern equivalent: Spanish silver coins] from the wrecked yacht Grooten Broeck, according to the order of the Honorable General and Council of India, to procure. In order to give this somewhat more weight, Captain Major Adriaen Anthonisz with 300 soldiers was sent back there to Batavia [Jakarta], however it was not obtained by the aforementioned Ducker regarding the restitution of the aforementioned money for that time, nor also with the further mission by the Honorable President Couckebacker from Batavia [Jakarta] there, inasmuch as the old King had died, and his son, the rightful heir, had been forced against certain conspirators to obtain possession by the sword, consequently he did not consider himself obligated to the Company. What advance in Quinam to make, in Joncquijn [uncertain: location], Cambodia [Camboidja], inasmuch as this happened before his time, and the beach lord who had struck the money was punished by death for such and other matters more, according to good founded reasons or the Honorable General's letter and some threats of the same in the form of reprisal to recover, not willing to listen, giving as answer that if we wanted to exercise trade, his land stood open to us, and if we wanted to begin war against him, he was ready to defend his kingdom with weapons. The aforementioned Ducker, seeing that he could not proceed in this matter, had charged to the accounts of the aforementioned Nicolaes Coeckebacker

--- CHUNK 1 ---
was punished more severely, according to well-founded reasons or the Honorable Lord General's missive and certain threats from the same, by way of reprisal to recover it, not wishing to listen, giving as answer that if we wished to exercise trade his land lay open to us, and if we wished to wage war against him he was prepared to defend his kingdom with weapons. The aforementioned dukker, seeing that he could not proceed in this matter, had charged to the account of the aforementioned Nicolaes Coeckebacker according to our order his senes and further capital against approximately 300 picol [modern equivalent: approximately 18 metric tons] of quinams, Tonquinese goods, and a small portion of Chinese silk as well as silk fabrics and little brown sugar with an advance of approximately 20,000 guilders on the senes that fell due, which aforementioned quinams return to Japan yielded well over one hundred percent profit, and the aforementioned dukker declared that yearly approximately 200,000 guilders in senes and beeswax could be debited there with an advance of 40 to 50 percent, and against yellow raw silk as silk goods to be traded. So that the quinams trade, which previously seemed to be of little value, now that the Japanese may no longer appear before the Company's gate, shows itself to be quite profitable, for these aforementioned 200,000 guilders advanced in quinam and up to 280 to 300 guilders, and as above being invested in raw silk and silk goods, would within a year in Japan yield little less than six tons of gold [modern equivalent: approximately 6,000 guilders], upon which having been carefully considered by us and the council to not overlook profits where profit is to be made, we have once again resolved to resume this trade, and have ordered the Honorable Coeckebacker that in Japan he shall see to gathering approximately 200 guilders in senes and approximately 1,500 to 1,600 picol of beeswax, notwithstanding that the Honorable Lord Geurt and the council of India had ordered that the aforementioned trade be

--- CHUNK 2 ---
tons of gold [modern equivalent: approximately 6,000 guilders], upon which having been carefully considered by us and the council to not overlook profits where profit is to be made, we have once again resolved to resume this trade, and have ordered the Honorable Coeckebacker that in Japan he shall see to gathering approximately 200 guilders in senes and approximately 1,500 to 1,600 picol of beeswax, notwithstanding that the Honorable Lord Geurt and the council of India had ordered that the aforementioned trade be abandoned by refusal of the aforementioned 23,580 rixdollars [modern equivalent: rixdollars] on its account, which we trust we shall have done well, just as the Honorable Lord Gewel and the council of India have been pleased to approve. I doubt not whether the Tonquinese trade (where yearly 800 to 1,000 picol of yellow raw silk falls, and by extraordinary harvests sometimes 1,500 to 1,600 picol) shall indeed be as profitable as the aforementioned quinams business, in view of the fact that silk there fetches a much better price and sometimes up to 60, 70, 80, and at the highest 100 taels [modern equivalent: taels] per picol can be obtained, of which in the month of January or February last past with a capital of approximately 150,000 guilders the Company's yacht Grol Godt the foremost a trial was taken, and the desired success with the next returning ships is to be expected. Considering the aforementioned imperial mandate in Japan, so is now also principally the Cambodian trade of Hertevellen, Cambodian nutmegs, lac, as well as other more merchants in Japan and other places placed in our charge, for which reason by the Honorable Lord Geurt and the council of India on the date of the 17th of April last the yacht Oudewater with a capital amounting to approximately 80,000 guilders was sent there, to take a trial of what business can be conducted there, but because of the missing of the river and late appearance of ours above the King's gate, as well as that a Japanese junk

--- CHUNK 3 ---
Hertevellen, Cambodian nutmegs, lac, as well as other more merchants in Japan and other places placed in our charge, for which reason by the Honorable Lord Geurt and the council of India on the date of the 17th of April last the yacht Oudewater with a capital amounting to approximately 80,000 guilders was sent there, to take a trial of what business can be conducted there, but because of the missing of the river and late appearance of ours above the King's gate, as well as that a Japanese junk remained there over a monsoon, by which everything had been purchased and departed, so our merchants could not make a shipment to Japan from there. When ours were received at court and well received, what good appearance for the same business they had, and how the aforementioned Oudewater in December fully laden with rice, lesser weir, benzoin and shellac returned again to Batavia, the expeditions undertaken at Mattauw Werf, the masters' fire and the timber spared further punishment excused and admonished to the continuation of good conduct: the Honorable Lord General's missive is amply made known to you, for which reason to avoid much unnecessary writing we shall refer ourselves to the aforementioned missive and come to the discussion of what has been advanced and occurred in Taiwan with the land expeditions undertaken. Upon our repeated requests to the Honorable Lord General and council of India to suppress the arrogance of the inhabitants of Mattauw, Soulang, Taccareijangh, and other more villages located on Formosa, and to punish as merited the massacre committed against ours in the time of Lord Nuijts, and shortly thereafter perpetrated by those of Taccareijangh, so were we, as you have previously advised, the requested 400 soldiers in the latter part of August in the year 1635 with the Honorable Adriaen Anthonisz, Captain Major of Batavia, sent, but because the weather at that time was still very rainy, the aforementioned expeditions had to be postponed until the month

--- CHUNK 4 ---
located on Formosa, and to punish as merited the massacre committed against ours in the time of Lord Nuijts, and shortly thereafter perpetrated by those of Taccareijangh, so were we, as you have previously advised, the requested 400 soldiers in the latter part of August in the year 1635 with the Honorable Adriaen Anthonisz, Captain Major of Batavia, sent, but because the weather at that time was still very rainy, the aforementioned expeditions had to be postponed until the month of November, when on the 23rd of the same month for sufficient reasons and motives with the council's approval the largest, most powerful, and most culpable village of Mattauw, with 500 white soldiers, and about 100 inhabitants of Sinckan were first attacked in the most unexpected manner, which succeeded so luckily and prosperously that on the date at about half an hour before sunset the same, without much resistance being offered, with a loss of 25 to 30 of theirs and not one wounded of ours, was very victoriously taken, and they lodged there that night. The next day, being the 24th of the same month, they marched with the entire train through the whole village, the houses were burned, which they had in great numbers, and the grain stores, setting them all on fire, and sparing the timber as much as possible to lure them back to their village and bring them to obedience. This accomplished, they then marched to the village of Baccaluan [Backaluan], which is located halfway between Mattauw and Sinckan, where we lodged that night, these were indeed also guilty of the aforementioned murder, but had been punished for it before this date, and had since conducted themselves reasonably well, so that we showed them our power only once, and our people refreshed themselves somewhat, leaving the inhabitants who had mostly fled at the first arrival to fetch straw and other necessities for the people: in which they showed themselves very helpful and willing. The next day, being the 25th of the same month, they had the entire community of Baccaluan come together with the others, and through Dr. Junij explained to them in the Sinckan language why Mattauw had been attacked, and sparing them on the hope that they would conduct themselves well (which they also promised to do), they marched to Sinckan where one of the most notable and most culpable of the aforementioned murder still in arms for the Company was by a Sinckan person beheaded as an example to others, and they marched forth with the people having eaten something to Saccam, where they lodged that night, and on the 26th of the same month having embarked in champans they returned in the morning to Coaijonan with this fortunate victory (for which thanks must be given to the Almighty) arrived. The people having refreshed themselves and in the meantime those of Mattauw with the instruction of the ownership of their lands to the Dutch state having been received again in grace, they marched on the 22nd of December with the aforementioned 500 white soldiers mostly well-trained, and about 400 to 500 inhabitants of the villages Sinckan, Soulang and Baccaluan to the village of Pagcareijang where Formosa: Saccareijangh was taken and entirely burned with fire, after long marching (having passed many beautiful flat fields, small woods and small rivers as well as some large rivers) on the 25th of the same month

--- CHUNK 1 ---
having taken their lands again into the grace of the Dutch state, they marched on the 22nd of December with the aforementioned 500 white-clad, mostly well-trained soldiers, and approximately 4 to 500 inhabitants from the villages of Sinckan, Soulangh, and Baccaluan toward the village of Pagcareijang, where Formosa [Taiwan] was taken and completely burned with fire. After we had marched for a long time (having passed through many beautiful flat fields, small woods, and small rivers, as well as some large rivers), we arrived on the 25th of the same month around midday, and encountered some troops of theirs, who at first came very fiercely at our people and the front troop, but seeing some of theirs fall underfoot and be wounded, they began to retreat into the long reeds and some fled toward the village. Thereupon their pursuers followed and took the village, which that same evening was set on fire to prevent the escape or withdrawal of the inhabitants and to prevent serious plundering from occurring. We made our camp in the flat field, where there was an abundance of long reeds and grass. According to the account that the Chinese and the Formosans themselves gave us afterward, 13 of theirs remained dead and 6 were wounded, although our inhabitants had obtained no more than 9 heads, which this nation is extremely eager for. None of ours remained, and only 2 or 3 soldiers were wounded in the feet with foot traps. The next day, being the 26th of the same month, we marched again toward Saccam, passing through the aforementioned village, which was located about a quarter hour's journey from an extraordinarily large or broad but shallow river. We found everything burned, with not a single house remaining standing, and as a certain sign that the inhabitants of the aforementioned village had surprised and murdered one of our Junks [small ships] lying in the Jouckan River at night,

--- CHUNK 2 ---
